To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

exercise training results in a persistent and marked improvement in insulin action on skeletal muscle glucose uptake, and that this is likely due to changes in the activity of signalling proteins that regulate skeletal muscle glucose uptake.

(i) exercise training increases insulin action in skeletal muscles from insulin‐resistant subjects, and this is due to changes in the activity of proteins involved with the regulation of glucose and lipid metabolism in skeletal muscle; (ii) the molecular mechanisms by which exercise training improves insulin action in skeletal musculature are not completely understood; and (iii) the molecular mechanisms that result from chronic exercise training are likely to be related to changes in protein expression and activity, which may include proteins involved with insulin signal

exercise training increases skeletal muscle glucose transport and oxidation, which is associated with increased insulin sensitivity in obese and insulin‐insensitive individuals, and that the molecular mechanism(s) underlying this effect are related to increased expression of proteins involved with the regulation of glucose metabolism and insulin signal transduction, and increased expression of proteins associated with lipid oxidation and mitochondrial biogenesis in skeletal muscle.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular basis of the insulin sensitizing effects of exercise in skeletal muscle.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms by which exercise training improves glucose homeostasis and insulin action in skeletal muscles of individuals with insulin resistance.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms that result in exercise training‐induced increases in insulin action in muscle from obese and type 2 diabetic individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

exercise training results in improved insulin sensitivity in insulin‐resistant and obese individuals by increasing the capacity of skeletal muscle to take up glucose and by improving lipid oxidation and/or utilization.
the molecular mechanism for exercise‐induced improvements on insulin action are complex and involve multiple signalling pathways and proteins in skeletal muscle.
exercise training improves insulin sensitivity by increasing the expression and/or activation of signalling proteins involved in glucose and lipid metabolism in skeletal muscle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exercise training is a potent and effective intervention for improving insulin action and reducing the risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
exercise improves insulin sensitivity by a number of molecular mechanisms.

the effects of exercise training on insulin action in skeletal muscles from obese individuals are mediated by a combination of increased lipid oxidation and turnover, and increased expression of proteins involved with insulin signal transduction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exercise training can improve skeletal muscle insulin action in insulin‐resistant and diabetic individuals.

the molecular mechanisms that mediate the beneficial effects of exercise on insulin resistance are likely to be different in the short‐term (i.e. 1–2 days after exercise) versus long‐term (i. e. 3–4 weeks after exercise training).
exercise training is a potent and safe strategy for improving insulin sensitivity, and this effect is likely due to changes in the activity of key signalling pathways in skeletal muscle.
